title: Access Modifiers, static, and Enums
summary: Protect fields with private and getters, share data with static, lock values with final, and model fixed choices with enums.
intro: A class is only as reliable as the rules it can enforce. This lesson shows how to hide fields behind methods, share data across every object with `static`, lock values with `final`, and model a fixed set of choices with an `enum`.

steps.title: Private fields and getters

example.title: Thermostat with a guarded setter
example.prompt: Keep a thermostat's temperature private, starting at 20, and ignore settings outside 10 to 30.
example.explanation: `temperature` is `private`, so `main` can only reach it through `getTemperature` and `setTemperature`. The setter checks the range before it assigns, so 35 and 5 are ignored and the value stays 24. The field starts at a valid 20 and every change goes through the setter, so code outside the class has no way to break the rule.

practice.title: Player health
practice.prompt:
Finish a Player class whose health is private and can never drop below 0.

1. Make `getHealth` return the private `health` field.
2. Make `takeDamage(int amount)` subtract `amount` from `health`, stopping at 0 instead of going negative.
3. Leave `main` as it is: it prints the health, takes 20 damage, then 45 damage.

Expected output:

```text
Ana: 50
Ana: 30
Ana: 0
```
hints: A getter just returns the field.
Work out `health - amount` first. If that is below 0, store 0 instead.
`Math.max` can pick the larger of two values in one step.

steps.title: Static vs instance

example.title: Numbered tickets
example.prompt: Count every Ticket created with a static counter and give each ticket its own id.
example.output:
Tickets: 0
Ticket #1 for Ana
Ticket #2 for Ben
Ticket #3 for Cy
Tickets: 3
example.explanation: There is one `count` for the whole class, and it starts at 0 before any ticket exists, which is why `Ticket.getCount()` works on the first line. Each constructor call bumps the shared `count` and copies its new value into that ticket's own `id`. `getCount` is static, so it is called on the class name. It could not read `id` or `owner`, because a static method has no object.

practice.title: Order totals
practice.prompt:
Track how many orders exist and the total of all their amounts in static fields.

1. In the `Order` constructor, add 1 to the static `count` and add `amount` to the static `total`.
2. Make the static methods `getCount` and `getTotal` return those shared values.
3. Leave `main` as it is: it creates three orders, prints each, then calls both static methods on the class.

Expected output:

```text
Book: $12
Lamp: $30
Pen: $3
Orders: 3
Total: $45
```
hints: The constructor runs once per order, so it is the place to update the shared fields.
Use `count++` and `total += amount`, then return the fields from the static getters.

steps.title: Final fields and constructor chaining

example.title: Immutable money
example.prompt: Build an immutable Money class with two chained constructors, a ZERO constant, and a plus method that returns a new object.
example.output:
Price: $4.75
Tip: $2.00
Total: $7.25
Price is still $4.75
example.explanation: `new Money(2)` runs the one-argument constructor, which hands off to `this(2, 0)`, so both `final` fields are set in a single place. `ZERO` is a `static final` constant that holds a `Money` object, a safe starting point for a sum because nothing can change it. `plus` never changes `this`: it builds and returns a new `Money`, which is why `price` is unchanged at the end. `plus` can read `other.dollars` even though it is `private`, because `private` limits access by class, not by object. In the format, `%02d` pads the cents with a zero to two digits.

practice.title: Immutable colors
practice.prompt:
Finish an immutable Color class with a grayscale constructor and a WHITE constant.

1. Make the one-argument `Color(int gray)` constructor chain with `this(...)` so red, green, and blue all equal `gray`.
2. Make the `static final` constant `WHITE` a gray of 255.
3. Make `mix(Color other)` return a new `Color` whose red, green, and blue are each the average of the two colors, using integer division by 2. It must not change either color.

Expected output:

```text
rgb(255, 165, 0)
rgb(128, 128, 128)
rgb(255, 255, 255)
rgb(255, 210, 127)
```
hints: The grayscale constructor is one line: `this(gray, gray, gray);`.
`WHITE` can use the grayscale constructor too.
In `mix`, average each channel with `(red + other.red) / 2` and pass all three to `new Color(...)`.

steps.title: Enums

example.title: Drink sizes
example.prompt: Define a Size enum with a price, list every size with its ordinal, name, price, and a label, then look one up by name.
example.output:
0 SMALL $3 (a little cup)
1 MEDIUM $4 (the usual)
2 LARGE $5 (a big one)
Picked: MEDIUM
Is medium: true
example.explanation: `Size.values()` walks the constants in the order they are declared, and `ordinal()` numbers them from 0. Each constant was built once by the enum's constructor, so `getPrice()` reads its own `price`. The switch in `label` uses bare names and covers all three constants, so it compiles with no `default`. `valueOf("MEDIUM")` returns the existing constant, which is why `==` is true.

practice.title: Turning right
practice.prompt:
Give a compass Direction its heading in degrees and turn it right four times, starting from NORTH.

1. Give `Direction` a `private final int degrees` field, a constructor that sets it, and a `getDegrees()` method. NORTH is 0, EAST is 90, SOUTH is 180, and WEST is 270.
2. Write `turnRight(Direction d)` as a switch expression with bare constant names and no `default`: NORTH goes to EAST, EAST to SOUTH, SOUTH to WEST, and WEST to NORTH.
3. In `main`, loop four times. Each time print `Turn <i>: <from> (<degrees>) -> <to> (<degrees>)` using `name()` and `getDegrees()`, then face the new direction.
4. Finally print `Back at start: ` followed by whether `facing == start`.

Expected output:

```text
Turn 1: NORTH (0) -> EAST (90)
Turn 2: EAST (90) -> SOUTH (180)
Turn 3: SOUTH (180) -> WEST (270)
Turn 4: WEST (270) -> NORTH (0)
Back at start: true
```

tests.output:
Turn 1: NORTH (0) -> EAST (90)
Turn 2: EAST (90) -> SOUTH (180)
Turn 3: SOUTH (180) -> WEST (270)
Turn 4: WEST (270) -> NORTH (0)
Back at start: true

hints: Build the enum like `Size` in the example: `NORTH(0)` and so on, a semicolon after the list, then the field, the constructor, and the getter.
Copy the shape of `label`: `return switch (d) { ... };` with one bare `case` per constant. The value each case returns still needs the type name, as in `Direction.EAST`.
Inside the loop, find the next direction first, print the line, then update `facing`.

recap:
- `private` hides a member from every other class. In one file, the other levels act alike. `protected` matters with inheritance.
- Keep fields `private` and expose `public` getters, plus setters or methods that validate before they change state.
- A `static` field has one copy shared by all objects. Call `static` methods on the class. They have no `this`.
- `final` fields are set once in the constructor. When no field can change, the class is immutable and its methods return new objects.
- Overload constructors and chain them with `this(...)` as the first statement. `static final` fields are class constants.
- Enums list fixed constants and can carry fields set by a constructor. Use `values()`, `name()`, `ordinal()`, `valueOf` (exact names only), and `==`.
- Switch on an enum with bare names like `case NORTH`. Covering every constant means no `default` is needed.
